# The Light-Leak

The camera arrived in a shoebox, which should have been my first warning. Mrs. Okafor handed it to me on her porch with the ceremony of someone passing over a newborn, and I accepted it the same way, cradling the weight of a Pentax Spotmatic from 1964, its leatherette worn smooth as river stone where forty years of thumbs had pressed.

"You'll want the neighborhood association to have real pictures," she said. "Not phone pictures. Phone pictures are for forgetting."

I didn't argue with her. She'd organized the Maple Street block party for twenty-two consecutive years, and I'd been assigned to document it because I'd once mentioned, at a meeting, that I'd taken a photography class in college. That was eleven years ago. I hadn't touched a real camera since.

The Spotmatic was heavier than I remembered cameras being. I loaded the film the night before—Mrs. Okafor had given me four rolls of Tri-X, expired in 2009, which she described as "still good, film is patient"—and I read the manual, which she'd also kept, its pages soft and yellow, annotated in her late husband's handwriting. *Meter wide open, then
